title: Modules, packages, internal/, and the cmd/ layout
summary: Go has two visibility levels, decided by the first letter of a name, plus internal/ directories that the go command enforces. Applications put binaries under cmd/ and everything else under internal/.

examples.title: Exported means "starts with an upper-case letter", and libraries obey it

annotations.note: No public or private keywords: Name and City are exported, password is visible only inside this package, in every file of it. There is no class-private or protected level.
encoding/json is another package, so it cannot touch password and silently leaves it out. A struct whose fields are all lower-case marshals to {} and never gets filled by Unmarshal.
fmt also uses reflection, but only reads, and it prints unexported fields too. Logging a struct with %+v can leak a secret that json.Marshal would have dropped.
reflect applies the same rule through StructField.IsExported. reflect.TypeFor[T]() (Go 1.22) gets the type without needing a value.

The spec says "a Unicode upper-case letter (category Lu)". İ is one, so İlçe is exported; dotless ı is lower-case. Names starting with _ or with a letter that has no case, such as 日, can never be exported. (The %-6s width counts runes, not bytes, so İlçe pads correctly.)

examples.title: cmd/ for binaries, internal/ for shared code, and an unexported name

annotations.note: A typical application module. Each directory under cmd/ is a package main that builds one binary named after the directory; keep main small (configuration, wiring) and put the logic in internal/.
Package vat's API is Of. round is an implementation detail that other packages cannot call, so it can change without breaking them.
Three packages, one module. A binary is addressed by its directory: go run ./cmd/shopd here, go install example.com/shop/cmd/shopd@latest for someone installing it from elsewhere.

go build ./... type-checks every package. cmd/peek reaches for an unexported function and fails to compile; the message names the rule. Importing internal/vat itself is fine: both packages live in example.com/shop.

examples.title: go.work joins two local modules; internal/ still stops outsiders

annotations.note: A library module and an app that uses it, both on disk. Without a workspace the app would need a require line and a published version, or a replace directive pointing at ../shop.
go.work: a go line and one use directive per module directory. go work init ./app ./shop writes this file for you; go work use adds more modules later.
No go.work yet, and app/go.mod doesn't require example.com/shop, so the import cannot be resolved. The error suggests go get, which would need a published module.
The go command looks for go.work in the current directory and its parents. Both modules are now main modules: the import resolves to the code on disk, with no edit to either go.mod.
internal/ is enforced across modules: only example.com/shop and the packages below it may import example.com/shop/internal/vat. A workspace does not lift that rule.

use_cases: Application: cmd/<binary>/main.go for each executable, internal/<feature>/ for the code, nothing importable by other modules
Library: the package at the module root (import example.com/lib), helpers in internal/ so you can change them without breaking users
Hiding a field or helper: start its name with a lower-case letter; the compiler enforces it at every use site in other packages
Developing a library and an app together: go work init ./app ./lib, without touching either go.mod
strengths: Visibility shows at every use site: shop.Gross is public and round is private without looking at a declaration, unlike Java modifiers or TypeScript export lists
internal/ is enforced by the go command, unlike Python's _module convention or a JS package's undocumented files
No build configuration: the directory tree is the package graph, so a new binary is a new directory under cmd/
go.work replaces the old habit of temporary replace directives in go.mod, which tended to get committed by accident
weaknesses: Only two visibility levels plus internal/: no protected and no class-private, so a struct's invariants are guarded from other packages but not from the rest of its own package
Changing visibility means renaming the identifier at every use site; gopls rename does it, plain search and replace may not
Import paths are absolute (module path + directory), so moving a package rewrites every import of it

pitfalls.title: Lower-case struct fields and encoding/json
pitfalls.detail: json.Marshal skips unexported fields and Unmarshal never sets them, without an error. Export the field and control its JSON name with a tag.

pitfalls.title: Printing structs that hold secrets
pitfalls.detail: fmt's %v and %+v print unexported fields. Give the type a String or slog LogValue method that redacts, or log selected fields only.

pitfalls.title: Assuming sub-directories share privileges
pitfalls.detail: example.com/shop/vat cannot see unexported names of example.com/shop. Nesting directories means nothing to the compiler; only the internal/ rule depends on paths.

pitfalls.title: Committing go.work
pitfalls.detail: A checked-in go.work can override a developer's own workspace and makes CI test versions users won't get. Keep it local, or run CI with GOWORK=off.

quiz.q: Which of these identifiers is exported?
quiz.why: İ (U+0130) is in Unicode category Lu, so İl is exported. _ is not a letter, and 日 has no case, so names starting with it can never be exported.

quiz.q: Module example.com/shop has a package in internal/vat. Who can import it?
options: example.com/shop and the packages below it
Any module in the same go.work
quiz.why: Code in or below internal/ is importable only by code rooted at internal's parent, here example.com/shop. A workspace does not change that.

quiz.q: json.Marshal(struct{ name string; Age int }{"Ayşe", 30}) returns?
quiz.why: encoding/json only sees exported fields; name is dropped without an error.

further_reading.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Exported identifiers
Tutorial: Getting started with multi-module workspaces

body:
## Concept

A package is a directory; every file in it declares the same package name and sees
everything the others declare. Across packages there are exactly two levels of
visibility, and the name itself says which: an identifier whose first character is
an upper-case letter is **exported**, anything else is visible only inside its
package. That covers types, functions, constants, variables, struct fields and
methods alike.

The go command adds one more rule based on paths: a package in or below a directory
named `internal` can be imported only by code rooted at the parent of that
directory. That is how a module keeps packages for itself while still splitting its
code into many packages.

The common layout follows from those two rules:

```
shop/                     module example.com/shop
├── go.mod
├── cmd/
│   ├── shopd/main.go     go build ./cmd/shopd  -> binary "shopd"
│   └── shopctl/main.go
└── internal/
    ├── orders/           example.com/shop/internal/orders
    └── vat/
```

A library puts its public package at the module root instead, so users import
`example.com/lib`, and keeps helpers in `internal/`. A workspace file, `go.work`,
lets several local modules build together while you change them in step.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Java**: exported ≈ `public`, unexported ≈ package-private. There is no `protected`
  and no class-private: every file in the package can touch a struct's lower-case
  fields. Like Java, `com.x.shop.vat` gets no special access to `com.x.shop`.
  `internal/` plays the role of packages a JPMS module does not export.
- **C/C++**: no headers to curate. Capitalization does what `static` and the header's
  contents do in C.
- **Python**: `_name` is a convention that anyone can ignore; Go's rule is checked by
  the compiler. There is no `__init__.py`: the directory is the package.
- **JS/TS**: the capital letter replaces the `export` keyword, `internal/` replaces a
  `package.json` `exports` map, and `go.work` resembles npm or pnpm workspaces.

## Design notes

Start with one package and split when a part has a clear name and API, by feature
(`internal/orders`, `internal/billing`) rather than by layer (`models`, `utils`).
Callers write the package name at every call, so `vat.Of` reads well and
`vat.VATOf` stutters. Import cycles are compile errors, which pushes the dependency
graph into layers whether you planned them or not. The official layout guide does not
use a `pkg/` directory; it is a community habit, and `internal/` gives the protection
`pkg/` only implies. Treat `go.work` as a local tool: it is for editing modules
together, and CI should build each module the way its users will (`GOWORK=off`).

example.com/shop/cmd/peek

example.com/shop/internal/vat

gross: 1200

# example.com/shop/cmd/peek
cmd/peek/main.go:9:31: name round not exported by package vat

$ go run .
main.go:6:2: no required module provides package example.com/shop; to add it:
	go get example.com/shop
-> exit status 1
$ go run .
gross: 1200

package example.com/app/sneaky
	sneaky/sneaky.go:3:8: use of internal package example.com/shop/internal/vat not allowed
